x: We refer to the action of some of the officials in not allowing J. Parker to run for us in the 3 miles event.
Parker, our new member from Brighton, was an entrant, and right from the start his huge stride took him into the lead. Tom Carter made a game effort to hang on but was plainly feeling it at the bell.
Parker (5,000 and 10,000 metres), A.
In "our" race, Parker and Penny finished together, as the appended result shows. The handicap was almost a complete triumph for our "under 21" brigade.

The result of the race was never in doubt, barring accidents, as Arthur Penny took the lead from the start, and gradually drew away from the field, eventually winning as he pleased. At the half-distance he was 55 secs. in front of Carter, with Parker next, having a very bad time, and hereabouts he retired.

Then a leg injury of Parker's asserted itself, and he began to drop places sensationally. Meanwhile, Footer was coming through the field at great speed, and eventually finished second, only two seconds behind Allum.
Parker, L.
As is usual the cracks set the pace, Penny, Cohen (who is showing improved form this year) leading, Ring, Taylor, Stimpson and Parker being bunched just behind.

As the Brook was in flood, the runners made a lap of the field (nearly a mile) to start, and at the end of this lap it was good to see about 18 runners well bunched together in spite of the fast pace set by Penny, Parker, Taylor and Co.
From the very start Pat Parker looked the winner and after the first mile he was leading, but followed very closely by Carter, Cohen, Stimpson and Ring, with the rest of the field in hot pursuit.

A further invitation having been given by the Union Sportive Metropolitaine for us to compete in the above event was accepted and the following team was chosen to represent the Club: Carter, Cohen, Footer, Patience D., Parker, Penny, Tobin and Verney, accompanied by W.

With such names as Penny, Footer, Ginty, Parker, D. Patience, Carter and Cohen to think of, it will be seen that we have every chance of success to bring the title where it has so seldom been in late years, namely the South.

This was handed over to Bill Lucas, who was brought into the "A" team owing to Pat Parker's non-arrival. He had to give ground to Ivor Brown, who ran very strongly; and Brickwood, for Mitcham, went off well in front of Arthur Penny.

The 9th April was dull but not particularly cold and 27 starters went off at the usual fast pace. Parker, who last year acted as pace-maker from start to finish and won easily, was not amongst the starters, but J.
Settling down to serious work after this very fast start, Pat Parker forged ahead with Tom Carter, Dan Patience and several others in close attendance.

Pat Parker made one of his rare appearances and although short of a little pep, finished 7th. Micky Walker ran well to gain 15th place and Jimmy Green was very pleased with himself and his 19th position.

Tom Wiley, who has been unable to compete much this season, showed us that he is still fit by gaining us valuable points in the Field Events, and helping us to win the Relay. We hope that Parker's Mile in 4.40 is a taste of things to come.

Some months ago Jack confided to the writer that he had been inspired and encouraged throughout his long career in athletics by the thought of some of our earlier Belgrave enthusiasts - men like Parker, Belchamber and Horwood - who had impressed him in those early 1920 days with their love of the sport and their Club.

Lord Parker, of New Malden, to whom much of the credit for the Belgrave Harriers' progress goes, was awarded his peerage in the Peace Honours List 'for distinguished services to Amateur Athletics and the public'.
The Captain that day was Bert Footer and the rest of the team were Allum, Carter, Flower, Ginty, Parker, Patience; Shaw, Ring, Rice, Shields and Taylor.
